# Copper June 2011 

- Copper continues to be a commodity that is not for the faint hearted as we draw the first half of the year to a close. For the past two months at least, we have noted the complete lack of conviction behind the metal’s price direction, and this sentiment has dragged on through June also, with average prices edging upward by a nickel to US$9031/t ($4.10/lb) (to the 24th).  Somewhat worryingly, the highest price point for the month (US$9171/t, $4.16/lb) came on the 1st, and ongoing concern over global economic woes have generally taken their bearish toll on commodity prices across the LME metals complex as the month has progressed. 

- Copper stays marginally above that psychological US$9000/t level for now, but it does not take too much bad news to push it below for the odd day or two at a time.  What forces it back up is the general view that anything below US$9000/t is considered cheap metal, but at this stage it should not be viewed as any particular endorsement of market conditions returning to a position of strength.  As the conditions behind these comments were largely in place in May, we have left our price forecast for this year unchanged at US$9586/t ($4.35/lb). 

- Last month we discussed the positive market specific developments that are leading to firmer demand in China and many of these have continued into this month.  That premia remain firm, stocks continue to edge lower and that the front month SHFE contract is in backwardation relative to the three month price all point to solid demand conditions. Why then, does market sentiment feel a good deal less sanguine than the above factors suggest?  In our view it is because of the as yet unknown scale of the slowdown that is required to get Chinese inflation under control and this partly explains our downgrade in to Chinese demand growth this year. 

- Perhaps inevitably after the very large surge in spot sales that occurred last month June was always likely to be relatively quiet by comparison.  In fact there was only one tender of note, emanating out of Mexico that secured terms in the mid 70s & 7s.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper prices edge up

by a nickel during June** Copper continues to be a commodity that is not for the faint hearted as we draw the first half of the year to a close.  For the past two months at least, we have noted the complete lack of conviction behind the metal’s price direction, and this sentiment has dragged on through June also. In May, a largely bearish tone won the day and that month’s average price of US$8926/t ($4.05/lb – cash) continued the mild downtrend of the prior two months. In June, average prices have edged upward by a nickel to US$9031/t ($4.10/lb) (to the 24th). But it has by no means been a convincing return to prices staying consistently above the $9000/t level, with the month’s low of US$8895/t ($4.03/lb) coming on the 13th and being in the middle of two days where prices were (marginally) above that psychologically important level.  Somewhat worryingly, the highest price point for the month (US$9171/t, $4.16/lb) came on the 1st, and ongoing concern over global economic woes have generally taken their bearish toll on commodity prices across the LME metals complex as the month has progressed. 

**IWCC comments set the tone for the month** The month got off to a poor start as it digested news on the final day of May from the International Wrought Copper Council that global copper demand growth for the period 2011-2012 would be merely half (8%) what it was during 2005-2010. With China having been responsible for much of that growth back then, given her annual double-digit expansion trajectory, it would inevitably be a hard act to follow. The IWCC’s belief that Chinese copper demand growth would only be c.7% this year effectively reinforced what we and many other have been saying, given that China has remained out of the market since her February New Year holidays.  Even so, to hear the IWCC’s Mark Loveitt put forward the arguments of high prices prompting substitution and economic uncertainty preventing Chinese buyers from returning to the market with any confidence summarised quite succinctly the handwringing that has been plaguing market makers for months. (Perhaps worse still, Loveitt was making these statements at an industry conference in Shanghai!) Following comments such as these, it was no surprise to see LME cash fall from what was May’s second highest price of the month of US$9224/t ($4.18/lb) on the 31st to US$9016/t ($4.09/lb) by June 3rd. 

**LME stocks “celebrate” a year’s high** At the same time as these IWCC comments were being delivered, it so happened that LME stocks rose above the 470kt level for the first time since June 4th 2010. The June-June low of 348.6kt reached on December 9th now seems so long ago, but to see also that part of the reason behind the rise in LME stocks has been exports from the stockpiles of the very country that most market watchers expected would be leading the way in direct consumption is particularly worrying for those who want to find any reassurance for buying the metal. 19.8kt cathode was exported fr

om China in May alone this year (more than Jan-May 2010 in total), bringing the fivemonth tally to 143.4kt, with much of it going into Asian LME depots. By the 9th, LME stocks had climbed to almost 478kt, but withdrawals brought that level back down to the 471kt mark by the 16th. We expect to see 465-470kt as we close out the month, broadly in line with early May and up c.90kt from the start of this year. #### **Weekly copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 1800 10000

Minor withdrawals from El Paso and Toledo brought overall metal stocks close to the 72kt (metric) level, from the month’s opening 74kt; the recent high of 77kt was seen on March 11th, but the fact that Comex closed out last year on under 60kt also shows some degree of market softening. This trend will likely continue until real demand picks up in China or a price arbitrage between the SHFE:LME becomes more attractive. Meanwhile, Chinese imports of refined copper cathode were almost 33% down to May _vs._ the five-month period for 2010, at 892kt, while scrap imports have been running at almost 5.5% up on Jan-May 2010, at 1.775Mt. But with scrap prices edging up slightly towards the end of the month, it is likely that this market is tightening now. #### **Copper spot premia ($/t)** 200 10

**Apparent statistical discrepancies remain with Chinese data** Back in our April issue, we reported on the apparent discrepancies between apparent refined copper consumption growth, semis output rates and end-use products output. Available production and trade data to May point to a contraction in apparent refined copper consumption of 8.6% yearon-year, with stock drawdowns clearly being a major feature of the Chinese copper market since late last year. Destocking in refined materials has also fed through to the semis sector, which appears to be underperforming end-use production by a considerable margin. Although we have always been aware of statistical differences between the principal sources of such data in China (the CNIA and the NBS) when it comes to _absolute_ tonnages, we now believe that the reason for the disconnect between the reported _growth rates_ in Chinese semis production _vs._ data comparisons with prior time periods is that the number of plants surveyed in the official statistics has been dramatically reduced this year. Previously, the financial cut-off for Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2011 Page 3 of 22 Copper Monthly Update semis plants to be included in the production survey was ~5M yuan in turnover. This year the cut-off has been raised to ~20M yuan. The year-on-year statistics now reflect a direct comparison of the new population of plants compared with this same population last year. However, there will be a very large drawback to this analysis during periods of extreme financial duress such as we see today because, almost certainly, the first plants to be forced to cut production or even shut down due to credit restrictions (compounded by high copper prices and negative arbitrage) will be the smaller plants with lower turnover that have the least robust cash flows and credit lines. We thus have a situation where the larger plants are almost certainly less affected by the current credit crunch and, more importantly, are taking up the slack from the smaller plants. Looking at the CNIA data to May, it appears that the new population of semis producers excludes over 15% of the prior production surveyed, and that a 10% decline in semis output in those plants that are no longer surveyed would have reduced the Jan-May semis growth figure under the old survey population to 13.5% from 19%, while a 20% reduction would give a growth rate of 12%. Ultimately, this year's semis production growth rates from both agencies are likely to be overstated, perhaps considerably because of these factors. **Power shortages may also impinge on semis manufactures this summer** Muddying the semis waters even further, looking ahead, will be the issue of power shortages during the summer months. Ongoing drought conditions, high coal prices and regu

lated power prices that have prevented many loss-making utilities from operating at full capacity already brought power shortages to some provinces during Q1 this year, and many provinces – including Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Anhui and Henan – have already implemented power cuts ahead of the usual summer starting date. #### **Semis output by provinces most at risk of power shortages** Others

Although China has experienced summer power cuts for many years, the last significant cutback was in 2004. However, the main difference between then and now is that semis producers’ order books were full and many of them switched to diesel self-generated power to cover the gap. This time around, with weaker order books, it may not be worth doing this. The chart above shows the province-by-province semis output for the first four months of this year, ranked according to size. Each province is also coloured either red, orange, purple or blue according to the potential severity of the impending power shortages. What the analysis shows is that 55% of semis production is in provinces that are determined to be in the "red zone" i.e. where cuts in excess of 4GW are possible, and a further 27% are in orange zone provinces where cuts could amount to 2-4GW. **Higher Chinese premia underscore increased appetite for copper** Despite this semis uncertainty, there are some indicators reflecting actual strength in Chinese copper markets. When cathode premia shot up in March from basement levels the previous month, the catalyst was not improving domestic demand but Japanese producers and traders seeking to meet delivery requirements following the earthquake and subsequent tsunami. A drop off in premia followed but in May premia were back up at high levels as demand picked up in line with improving Chinese semis output. In June, they remained at elevated levels of around $90/t. **European premia respond to cut in Russian exports** In Europe, the single most important influence on the cathode market this year has been the collapse in Russian exports of cathode since the imposition of the export tax by Russian authorities back in December. January-April cathode exports fell from over 166kt in 2010 to just over 61kt this year, and this reduction in what is typically standard quality material has forced many users to turn to Grade A and Chilean brands. Consequently, premia here have moved up from US$60/t at the end of March to $75/t by May; in June, these levels edged higher still, to $85. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2011 Page 4 of 22 Copper Monthly Update Meanwhile, in the USA, with rod production tailing off in May, and stocks of cathode and rod moving up, the main reason why p

remia have _not_ fallen this month from their May levels of 5.5-5.75c/lb has been the potential for one supplier to halt production if a labour contract was not renewed by its due expiration date of June 30th . However, with a 78% turnout, United Steelworkers members across Asarco’s five units in Arizona and New Mexico voted to accept the company’s offer (nine to one in favour) on June 23rd, and extend the existing contract for another two years. Consequently, we would not be surprised to see some regional premia weakness in the weeks ahead. **Macro economics and politics influencing prices more so than metal specifics** These regional minutiae aside, we continue to see that the main influences on the copper market these days are at the macro-economy level, with the Greek debt issue and concern over economic growth in both the USA and China keeping copper markets on a knife edge. The election of a new political regime in Peru – deemed immediately by the trading community a “worry” for supply, before producers themselves appealed for a more measured reaction – had the expected bullish then bearish impact on prices over the course of two days early in the month before giving way to economic matters elsewhere. The focus then turned to China, where the government may yet have to take further credit tightening measures in order to combat inflationary pressures; meanwhile in the US, job growth and widespread economic recovery remain elusive. Copper indeed stays marginally above that psychological US$9000/t level for now, but it does not take too much bad news to push it below for the odd day or two at a time. What forces it back up is the general view that anything below US$9000/t is considered cheap metal, but at this stage it should not be viewed as any particular endorsement of market conditions returning to a position of strength. As the conditions behind these comments were largely in place in May, we have left our price forecast for this year and 2012 unchanged at US$9586/t ($4.35/lb) and US$9588/t respectively. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

Last month we discussed the positive market specific developments that are leading to firmer demand in China and many of these have continued into this month.  That premia remain firm, stocks continue to edge lower and that the front month SHFE contract is in backwardation relative to the three month price all point to solid demand conditions. Moreover, with bonded stocks now down to levels where most of the material in warehouses is tied up in financing deals, and with an open arbitrage window, cathode ought to be flying into China in the coming months.  Why then, does market sentiment feel a good deal less sanguine than the above factors suggest?  In our view it is because of the as yet unknown scale of the slowdown that is required to get Chinese inflation under control and partly explains our downgrade in to Chinese demand growth this year. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Greece is the word** After having slipped off the front pages for a while, debt problems in the Euro area reared their ugly head again to send stock markets and the Euro currency crashing.  This should not augur well for consumer confidence across the region and as such ought to be bad for economic activity also.  However, every cloud has a silver lining and it would be churlish to dismiss the support that a weak currency provided in boosting exports and in doing so stimulating recovery in major industrial powerhouses like Germany in the aftermath of first stages of the ongoing debt crisis. 

**Western European economic outlook upgraded** Although the timing is a little unfortunate given the debt crises, we have actually upgraded our view on the economic outlook in Western Europe, compared to downgrades to other parts of the globe.  Indeed, Eurozone industrial production continues to increase at a healthy rate, particularly on a year-on-year basis, with April’s data revealing a 6.1% expansion even if the rate of month-on-month growth has eased a little.  For the year as a whole, we expect Eurozone IP to increase in the region of 5% in 2011 before easing to the 2-3% range for the following two years.  Germany is leading this growth and we estimate growth in IP of just over 9% this year, following on from double-digit growth in 2010. 

**Wire rod leads European demand** Without doubt it is the wire rod market that is leading demand in Europe, with rod makers continuing to report healthy market conditions.  Most rod producers expected demand strength to continue on from the strong end to 2010 and were set for continued growth but in most cases their

expectations have been exceeded so far this year. Certainly, we expect some slowing in activity in the second half of the year but are still looking for a major part of overall demand growth coming from wire rod. In fact, it is strong output of Russian wire rod that is driving a sharp upturn in our forecast for Russian refined copper demand this year. We have discussed previously our expectations for this following the re-imposition of a tax on cathode exports and latest trade data confirms our view. Russian exports of wire rod are up by over 130% at 116kt in the first four months of the year compared with the January-to-April period of 2010, while exports of refined copper have slumped by 61% to 65kt. As a result of the increased domestic production of wire rod and as such, higher demand for cathode, we expect consumption growth of over 50% to 700kt this year, before growth eases back to more sensible growth rates in the low single-digit range thereafter. Clearly this strong growth flatters our overall European demand estimate for this year. #### **Italian copper and copper alloy semis production (kt)** 40 360

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2011 Page 6 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Signs of substitution emerging elsewhere** While wire rod output drives overall demand higher, elsewhere some signs of slowing have emerged, with much of this easing being a result of the lofty copper price. In short, high prices are resulting in substitution of copper in some applications. At this stage, it would appear that substitution is merely tempering the rate of growth in demand for copper products, rather than causing outright contraction but without doubt, this is worrying development. **Italian semis output in modest Q1 gain** The strength of the European rod market has found its way into Italy but to a lesser degree than elsewhere, with Italian copper wire production up a solid, if not spectacular, 3.4% year on year in the first quarter. As elsewhere in Europe, it is rod that has led overall production higher, with copper semis output up by 1.7% year on year to 152.7kt, while copper alloy semis production edged up 1.4% to 141.8kt. Overall growth then came in at 1.6% for copper and copper alloy semis combined in the first three months of the year. **Second half slowdown to clip full year growth** For our latest quarterly update we have thoroughly reviewed first quarter apparent consumption data and this has led us to downgrade our full year view of refined metal demand in Western Europe. While we remain confident in the prospects for key markets such as Germany, its demand strength is being weighed down els

ewhere, particularly in southern Europe. Moreover, we have always expected a slowdown in demand growth in the second half of the year as economic activity slows. As such, we now expect Western European apparent consumption growth of 2.3% this year, before slowing further still in 2012. ### **Americas** **US copper demand robust in H1** With the improving US economy during the January-April period, US copper demand has remained pretty robust, especially in the wire markets, and it is only following the renewed discussion over economic downturn potential from May that there is now some concern over metal demand as we head into the summer months. Even so, to April copper rod production, which accounts for roughly 70% of primary refined copper consumption in the US, put in a sufficiently strong performance that we expect first half copper demand to be up by 3.8% on H1 2010 at 972kt. This follows the usual pattern of a strong first half in the US, with H2 down typically by 8-10% on H1 in most years of our analysis. Given the strength in demand so far, we expect this year will follow a similar pattern, leaving full year demand at 1.84Mt, or up by 4.6% on 2010. #### **US wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

**Copper rod output remains the driving force** Just as we were expecting the rod market to show signs of cooling down, April production data at least from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) revealed how well it has held up. At 110.4kt, rod output was marginally stronger than January’s 109.5kt, and we have to go back to last July to see a higher tonnage than this. Average monthly output this year to April, at 109kt, has edged out last year’s 105kt, and reflects the stronger automotive market. However, copper rod shipments in April fell by almost 7% on March at 107kt, pushing rod stocks back up to 24.6kt from 21.3kt held in March, and perhaps giving an early indication of the summer slowdown that we have been expecting. This came one step closer with the release of May rod sector figures in lateJune. Output, at 107.7kt, was 2.4% lower than April while shipments, at 103kt, were 3.7% down month-on-month. Furthermore, rod stocks, ending May at 29.4kt, surged by 16% from the prior month. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2011 Page 7 of 22 Copper Monthly Update **Housing market still issuing erratic data** Meanwhile, even the housing market has shown signs of bottoming out in some aspects. May housing starts were up by 3.5% on April and continue with the erratic up-down performance seen so far this year, while building permits for May were up by 8.7% on

April and were indeed the strongest seen since last December. However, there are still fundamental issues with the housing sector which will not be ironed out for a considerable period of time. As the building/construction sector tends to account for 40% of the total wire mill products market and takes a similar proportion of the overall tube and pipe produced for plumbing and heating tube, it is this sector which continues to act as the principal drag on copper’s recovery. **Building sector has some way to go before copper can pull itself up** To put the contribution of this building sector a little into context vis-a-vis the copper industry, ABMS data for the brass mills sector for full year 2010, which has just become available, does reflect an improvement in shipments on 2009 of almost 13%, at 980.4kt (metric). However, due to the Q4 2008 recession, even this 2010 performance remains 38% below the prior twelve-year average, and 16.5% below 2008 itself. In other words, although we anticipate demand growth in US copper demand this year, at a reasonable rate of 4-5%, it could be a lot better if the glut of housing hanging over the market could be run down – but this problem is not going to go away for many years yet. #### **US brass mill shipments (kt)** 20 100

### **China** **Indicators point to solid near term demand** Last month we discussed the positive market specific developments that are leading to firmer demand and many of these have continued into this month. That premia remain firm, stocks continue to edge lower and that the front month SHFE contract is in backwardation relative to the three month price all point to solid demand conditions. Moreover, with bonded stocks now down to levels where most of the material in warehouses is tied up in financing deals, and with an open arbitrage window, cathode ought to be flying into China in the coming months. Why then, does market sentiment feel a good deal less sanguine than the above factors suggest? In our view it is because of the as yet unknown scale of the slowdown that is required to get Chinese inflation under control, not to mention the threat of a power shortages hitting refined copper and or semis output in the coming months. We have discussed the potential for power shortages in the _Markets_ section of this report. **Bonded stocks with little further to fall** Stocks in Shanghai bonded warehouse were around 200-300kt at the end of June and we believe they will remain at these levels for the time being as most of this material is tied up in financing deals. With stocks now having little more to offer copper consumers, the shortfall from domestic c

athode production must surely come from imports, which so far this year have been a disappointment.  Indeed, cathode imports are down by a third in the first five months of 2011 but even worse was the near 800% surge in exports, which resulted in a less than stellar contribution to apparent consumption from net trade so far this year.  However, with the combination of declining stocks and lower exports in line with a more positive arbitrage position, net trade should provide more of a boost in the coming months. 

**Economic data paint a cloudy backdrop** With plenty of positives discussed above, it is only reasonable to highlight the less positive factors that are unfolding in the Chinese market, with most of these related to the economy.  At the head of worries are latest inflation figures for May, which rather than revealing a slowing in the rate of price rises, actually showed an acceleration.  Indeed, CPI picked up to 5.5% in May, the fastest pace of growth since 2008.  In almost a direct response, authorities yet again increased banks reserve requirement a further 50 basis points in mid-June to 



Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2011

21.5%.  At the same time, industrial activity, while slowing, isn’t grinding to a halt, with industrial output up by 13.3% in May, although this marks the slowest rate of growth this year.  This can be read two ways: either IP is slowing in response to higher interest rates which should lead to lower inflation and as such no further measures are required or inflation is continuing to surge ahead despite slowing industrial activity and suggesting further tightening measures are indeed required.  We are not overly concerned by the slowdown in IP as we expect full year growth to come in at around 13%, implying growth below this level in the second half of the year.  Inflation is a worry though and provides downside risk to demand growth. 

The major concern with higher inflation is that this results in further tightening measures from central bankers.  Firms are already finding it difficult to finance stocks as borrowing rates rise, with high copper prices making this doubly difficult, despite the recent modest respite that softer SHFE and LME levels have provided.  Moreover, it is typically small companies that find it hardest to access credit when credit is rationed but semis producers are typically small in scale, despite a few notable exceptions in China.  As such, higher lending rates disproportionately impact fabricators and add further downside risk to our demand outlook for this year and next. 

**Balancing act leans downwards overall** Despite the relatively bullish near term developments that we have discussed above, based on data to hand so far this year and expectations of slowing economic and industrial activity in the second half of the year, we have downgraded our full year estimate of refined copper demand this year to 5% growth from 6% previous

ly. However, we expect a rebound in 2012, with demand expanding by 7%. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

### **Japan** **Industrial output crawls off the bottom** Industrial activity in Japan has, unsurprisingly, dropped sharply since the devastating earthquake and tsunami in March. After falling by 15.5% month on month in March, industry grew by just 1.6% in April, as factories remained closed and supply chains disrupted. However, the country appears to have overcome much of this disruption, with surveys by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry showing that manufacturers expect to be back at pre-quake levels of production by July. Although power may still be a constraint through the summer, it does seem likely that Japanese industry will be able to recoup much of the lost ground in the second half of the year. Nevertheless, Wood Mackenzie expects activity for the year as a whole to be down by 2.1% from 2010. Continued recovery and the low base effect should enable growth to accelerate to 7.3% in 2012, before moderating down to a little over 2% in the following few years. **Shipments supported (for now) by rebuilding** Despite the slump in industrial output mentioned above, shipments have held up impressively. In fact, wire and cable shipments expanded by 3% year on year in May, although this masked an 8.9% month-on-month fall and even more worrying is that support from temporary building is about to run out of steam. It has been the building of temporary homes that has lifted demand from the construction sector and in doing so tempered weakness elsewhere. However, with temporary housing now complete, we expect shipments to the construction sector and those overall to slip back in the coming months. This is why we expect a decline in cathode demand in the second half of the year, despite wire and cable shipments being up 1.2% in the first five months of the year. **China’s 5M 2011 concentrate imports down by 15.5% on a year earlier** As has been the case in each month of this year, Chinese copper concentrate imports have failed to keep pace with each corresponding period of 2010.  During May 2011 official imports remained virtually unchanged over April’s level at 466kdmt, which while narrowing the gap to just -2.2% on the prior period still left cumulative receipts trailing by 15.5% or 431kdmt over the first five-months.  While imports from Chile, Peru and Australia have all declined thus far in 2011, Mexico has made significant gains (+63%) over last year, although it is unclear whether the customs data distinguishes between Mexican produced material from US shipments that were made through the Mexican port of Guaymas.  We had expected imports to pick up noticeably in July/August ahead of the start up of the new 200kt/a Zijin smelter but we now hear that commissioning will not occur until November which is a delay of three months. 

**China to close antiquated smelting technology** In keeping with the objectives in its new 5-year plan the Chinese government continues to introduce and indeed implement ever more stringent measures to improve energy efficiency and environmental conditions.  To this end, all antiquated copper smelters that employ blast, reverb

eratory or electric furnace technology are to be shut down by the end of this year. Although this is by no means a new initiative, the government does appear to be taking the enforcement of these measures far more seriously than in the past and has identified 291kt/a of copper smelting capacity that must shut by year end. Perhaps more important, is the government’s attitude towards greenfield smelting projects. Historically, it was not uncommon for copper smelting projects to have been constructed and commissioned with little or no regulation from local, regional or central governments. Today the situation has changed quite profoundly in that there is no longer a lax attitude towards these developments. This now means that for any smelter project, its environmental impact assessment statement has to be approved by the relevant environmental authority prior to any construction being initiated. We have identified almost 2.7Mt/a of primary Chinese smelter project capacity awaiting such approval with no guarantee of this being granted. Clearly this has major implications for the custom smelting market as a whole given that China is the largest consumer of internationally traded concentrates and the country is also viewed as the key engine of capacity growth in this market. Given the significant additions to copper in concentrate supplies over the next few years any deferral or stalling of primary smelter capacity growth will accelerate what appears to be inevitable, i.e. a reversal of the long-established trend of copper concentrate market deficits into surpluses. #### **Chinese Primary Smelter Capacity – (kt Cu)** 7000

## Production news 

**2011 mine output forecast cut by 71kt** A combination largely of bad weather and labour relations issues have brought about a 71kt cut in our mined copper forecast for this year since our last report from 16.852Mt to 16.781Mt (prior to market adjustments), all of it in the “western world”.  Chilean operations have taken the brunt of this reduction, with 60kt lost from national output over the past month.  Here, we have seen Antofagasta reduce its output target at Esperanza for a second time this year to between 80-100kt, down from the 165kt expected in Q1 this year and 130kt revised target of a month ago.  The second operation for losses this month has been a contractor’s strike at Codelco’s El Teniente, which took hold in the first week of this month and at one stage reduced operations to 40% of capacity.  The company has since reportedly brought that figure up to 90% or so, but we estimate that around 20kt of copper contained in concentrate output has been lost through the dispute, and we have now pegged El Teniente back to c.410kt as a result. 

Elsewhere in Chile, no single issue has plagued one particular operation during the month; instead, several small outages, ranging from management-labour discontent at Codelco’s Chuquicamata to heavy rains at BHPB’s Escondida, have halted operations for half a day or so, and as such were more “market-related” events carrying some short-term potential for supporting LME prices rather than becoming any meaningful disruption to the supply stream.  Equally, the June 20<sup>th</sup> earthquake reported 90km north east of Calama was sufficiently deep underground not to have affected any of the mining operations in the region. 

Meanwhile, better than expected output from Mexican operations pushed national output there up by 15kt to partially offset the Chilean losses from a Latin American regional perspective, but mildly lower output from operations in Zambia (- 15kt since last month), Australia and Papua New Guinea (-10kt each) all contributed to that net 70kt loss.

**Zambian output falls by 10% to April** In Zambia, a challenging rainy season has reduced national mine output in April by almost 10% this year to 242kt _vs._ 266kt in the same period of 2010.  Although we believe that some of this output will be made up during the second half of the year, we do not think that this will entirely be the case and have cut our forecast output by 15kt accordingly, to 750kt.  Even so, this figure would represent a 10% year-on-year increase in mined output, with the most important gains being made at First Quantum’s expanding Kansanshi operations.  Here, mined copper output rose by 21% during Q1 and we are expecting an overall increase of 15% this year to c.270kt copper contained in sulphide concentrate and via the SxEw route.  First Quantum will play a significant role in Zambia’s nearterm copper production growth, not just because of its Kansanshi expansion but also because of its Trident project (formerly known as Kalumbila), which could add as much as 150kt/a copper in the first stage of development alone. However, it is likely that a new smelter would be required, given the unfavourable economics of exporting concentrate (including a 15% export tax) and because by that time (2014-2015) existing smelter space would be fully utilised.  (For a more complete review of Zambian copper operations, see our Insight: “Zambia – back to former glories” released earlier this month.) 

**New smelters are the talk of the day** Despite the apparent logic and ultimate need for additional smelting capacity in Zambia (even on top of the mere three-year old Chambishi NFC unit), the economics behind building new smelter capacity in general in the traditional western world make such an investment difficult to justify financially.  Only last month did Xstrata announce the closure of smelting and refining capacity in Australia, citi

ng a poor economic outlook for that processing part of the business.  Yet, since early May, we have had three other greenfield smelter plans being aired as well as a brownfield expansion confirmed.  The latter is in Iran, where Outotec plans to expand NICICO’s Sarcheshmeh by 2014 from the current 130kt/a to 280-300kt/a by replacing the old reverb furnaces with a new flash smelter in order to accommodate higher planned mine output going forward as well as to improve environmental conditions from the existing plant. 

In China, Yunnan Copper says it will establish a 100kt/a capacity smelter, although details of when and which source materials (primary or secondary) have yet to be revealed (its copper refinery expansion announcements of late have been tied to its captive blister product from the Chambishi NFC plant in Zambia).  And China’s Shandong Liaocheng Yanggu province intends to establish a new copper industrial park with 0.9Mt smelting and refining processing capacity (plus copper products), with Shandong Xiangguang reportedly being asked to spearhead the effort.  Shandong already has the capacity to produce c.400kt/a primary copper (with plans to raise that by 50% by 2014) plus 50-70kt/a secondary copper. 

For the Zambian and Iranian plans, there is clearly some logistical and financial rationale for such smelter investments, and for the Chinese proposals, we would need additional details to comment.  But the remaining publicly-announced plan – that of Norilsk Nickel to build a copper smelter in Indonesia – is a little baffling.  In early May, Norilsk signed an MoU with Indonesia’s Nusantara Smelting Corp to work on studies for a 400kt/a copper smelter.  Although the company says it will develop copper (and nickel) resources in the country to supply the smelter, Indonesia already has excess smelting capacity relative to its metal consumption and is geographically close to the two countries in the world (China/India) which have been partly responsible for the low TCRCs that we have witnessed over the last couple of years.  Such a comprehensive plan for semi-integrated facilities (there was no mention of establishing a refinery) would therefore only make sense in the very distant future.
